title: Day-zero lab: private control plane deploy and Terraform quirks
body:
Purpose and scope:
This doc is a lab-style, day-zero run log for commissioning a Private Control Plane (PCP) in a VPC / on-prem environment. It captures the exact sequence we used in the lab, Terraform module observations (quirks and workarounds), a conservative upgrade/rotation choreography tested here, and the lightweight verification suite we used to validate each step.

Audience:
- Operators preparing the first customer-private control-plane deployment
- Infra engineers writing Terraform modules or CI that manages customer CPs
- SREs who run rotation/upgrade drills and want concrete commands and failure cases

Assumptions for this lab run:
- Target environment: AWS VPC with private subnets (no public IPs on CP nodes) and a customer-managed KMS key in the same account.
- Base AMIs with secure kernel + required NVMe drivers installed.
- Terraform state stored in S3 bucket with DynamoDB lock table (tfstate-privcp-lab).
- We used terraform-provider-aws v4.x and our in-house terraform modules at tag v2025.11.

High-level sequence performed:
1) Prep network and KMS artifacts
2) Bootstrap seed cluster (ephemeral single-node) for initial control-plane components
3) Apply Terraform modules for control plane (k8s control plane services, etcd, api ingress)
4) Smoke validation and KV cache sanity check
5) Simulated scale-up (add CP nodes) and controlled rotation (replace one node at a time)
6) Post-change validation and rollback tests

Detailed steps and commands (abridged):
- Network & IAM:
  - Create dedicated VPC Peering + route tables for customer project. Tagging conventions: rw:cp:<customer>-env.
  - KMS alias: alias/rw-privcp-<customer>-kek. Policy must allow STS:AssumeRole from platform account.

- S3/Dynamo Terraform backend config (example):
  terraform {
    backend "s3" {
      bucket = "rw-privcp-tfstate"
      key    = "<customer>/control-plane/terraform.tfstate"
      region = "us-west-2"
      dynamodb_table = "rw-privcp-locks"
      encrypt = true
    }
  }

- Bootstrap notes:
  - We intentionally started with an ephemeral seed node to minimize blast radius. Seed is not part of final cluster; its role: produce initial certs and etcd snapshot for controlled import.
  - Command used to snapshot etcd and transfer: etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-seed-$(date +%s).db (scp to operator workstation)

Terraform module observations (quirks + workarounds):
- Module: rwcp-network (v1.7.2)
  - Quirk: auto-generated route table names sometimes exceed AWS name length limits when customer names are long -> we added a short-hash suffix in the module. Workaround in module: var.name_prefix_trunc = substr(var.name_prefix, 0, 12).

- Module: rwcp-etcd (v1.4.0)
  - Quirk: etcd ASG lifecycle hooks race with cloud-init provisioning. If node boots slowly due to NVMe format, etcd cluster sees partial membership and tries to elect prematurely.
  - Workaround: add a pre-start systemd unit that waits for disk-ready and ensures kubelet starts only after /var/lib/etcd is mounted. We added a 30s backoff loop.
  - Import trick: when recovering from a seed snapshot, import etcd instance IDs into state via terraform import module.rwcp-etcd.aws_autoscaling_group.etcd asg-xxxxx. Keep a mapping file locally (TF_IMPORT_MAP).

- Module: rwcp-controlplane (v2.0.0-alpha)
  - Quirk: the module exposes a map of OIDC client IDs which Terraform flattens unpredictably between plan/apply (because of computed values).
  - Workaround: pin provider version and set lifecycle.ignore_changes on the map in most customer stacks; treat client creation as a separate apply step via a small wrapper module.

State migration and import notes:
- When we moved from the lab prototype to the production-like module shape we had to remap resource addresses. Use a two-step plan: first apply a shim module that creates new resources with temporary names, terraform state mv the old addresses to new addresses, then apply the true module after verifying resources are present. Keep a state backup for each mv: aws s3 cp s3://rw-privcp-tfstate/<customer>/control-plane/terraform.tfstate ./tfstate-backup-<ts>.json

Scaling choreography tested (safe sequence):
1) Add new CP node to ASG with user-data that includes join-token from KMS-encrypted secret.
2) Wait for healthcheck: platform health endpoint /internal/health returns OK for 5 consecutive checks spaced 10s apart.
3) Verify KV cache state: run rw-cpctl cache-check --summary and ensure prefix hit ratio within expected delta.
4) Drain an old node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
5) Confirm control-plane endpoints stable (no >2s p95 API latency spike for >1m).

Rotation (certs + KMS key rotation) choreography:
- Goal: rotate KEK without causing ETCD auth break or API downtime.
- Steps tested in lab:
  1) Create new KMS key in same account, replicate key policy from existing key (keep alias alias/rw-privcp-<customer>-kek-new).
  2) Gradual re-encryption: fetch secrets, re-wrap with new key into a new secret path (secrets/new-key/*).
  3) Update configmap/secret ref in control-plane deployment to reference new secret path.
  4) Rolling restart of control-plane pods one-at-time with a preStop hook: sleep 15s and flush any in-memory caches to disk.
  5) Monitor etcd leader changes and API latency; if >3 leader elections within 10m, abort and roll back to old key.

Notes on KMS cross-account and HSM:
- If customer uses an external HSM/KMS (Azure Key Vault / on-prem HSM), our module expects a simple wrapping API endpoint. In the lab we stubbed the HSM with a tiny service that signs and unwraps with predictable latencies. Real world: include a 50-100ms latency fudge factor when computing API timeouts in service mesh sidecars.

Failure scenarios and observed behaviors:
- Failed node replace mid-etcd-join: etcd membership left a tombstone entry. Remediation: run etcdctl member remove <id> from leader and rejoin with a clean snapshot. Make sure the Terraform module's ASG doesn't re-add the tombstoned ID by clearing the launch template user-data's static member ID references.

- Terraform plan drift after manual cert rotation: If operator rotated certs outside Terraform, computed resources cause plan to try to re-create. Mitigation: record manual changes into a short-lived tfpatch resource (module.rwcp-certs.null_resource.manual_rotation) and then remove after next apply, OR better: create a small provider-ext-managed flag documenting the rotation.

Lab verification suite (commands we used after each major change):
- rw-cpctl status --format=summary  # quick health summary
- curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_TOKEN" https://api.privcp.local/internal/health | jq .
- kubectl get cs,componentstatuses -A
- etcdctl --endpoints=<endpoints> endpoint status
- python tests/smoke/test_ingress_and_tokens.py::TestIngress::test_token_rotation

Rollback play (fast rollback):
- If new control-plane nodes fail to reach Ready within 10m or API p95 spikes > 3s for >5m:
  1) Terraform destroy module.rwcp-controlplane.new_nodes (or revert ASG desired capacity to previous value)
  2) Reintroduce old user-data / old KMS secret refs via terraform apply with pinned module version
  3) If etcd state corrupted, restore from last known good snapshot: etcdctl snapshot restore <good-snapshot>.db --initial-cluster=... then import states as described above.

Open questions & follow-ups (items to turn into tickets):
- Do we want to bake a small etcd resilience probe into the node user-data that fails startup if snapshot import doesn't complete? (Ticket: CP-xxxx)
- Add support in rwcp-etcd module for gradual membership replacement (automatic tombstone purge + rehydrate) without operator tf state mv. (RFC + ticket)
- Handle Terraform provider computed maps in rwcp-controlplane module more deterministically (we should add stable computed keys and an exported list for downstream modules).

Action items from this lab:
- Lina: create TF shim module and a test that runs terraform state mv in CI and verifies the mapping (due: 2026-02-17).
- Marco: add the disk-ready pre-start unit to the official AMI build pipeline and add smoke test for NVMe formatting (due: 2026-02-24).
- Maeve: write the minimal KMS cross-account latency guide and include recommended API timeouts in platform defaults (due: 2026-03-03).

Appendix: helpful snippets used in lab (copied here so operators don't hunt in history):
- terraform import example:
  terraform import module.rwcp-etcd.aws_autoscaling_group.etcd asg-0a1b2c3d4e5f

- etcd snapshot restore (safe mode):
  export ETCDCTL_API=3
  etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-snap.db
  etcdctl snapshot restore /tmp/etcd-snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-from-snap --name new-etcd-1 --initial-cluster new-etcd-1=https://10.0.1.10:2380 --initial-cluster-token rw-privcp-restore

- quick health-check script (example):
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -euo pipefail
  for i in {1..5}; do
    curl -fsS https://api.privcp.local/internal/health -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_TOKEN" && break || sleep 10
  done

Final note: this doc intentionally contains lab log artifacts and transient commands. Before applying any of these steps to a customer production environment, convert the snippets into curated runbook steps and add required guardrails (explicit timeouts, irrevocable change review, and a canary traffic policy).

If you want a follow-up, I can:
- extract the TF import map we built (TF_IMPORT_MAP) and attach as a CSV
- produce a step-by-step minimal runbook (no lab noise) for customer onboarding

-- Ravi K.
